Ernest Shackleton was an Irish polar explorer whose expeditions to the South Pole and Antarctica produced some of the most dramatic survival stories in exploration history. Though he never achieved his greatest geographic goals, his leadership during the Endurance expedition earned him lasting fame. When his ship became trapped and crushed by pack ice in 1914, and the expedition seemed doomed, Shackleton brought every one of his twenty-eight crew members back alive.

He first participated in Robert Falcon Scott's Antarctic expedition from 1901 to 1903, and came close to the South Pole before illness forced him to return. He led his own attempt in 1907 and 1909, reaching a new record of eighty-eight degrees twenty-three minutes south—just ninety-seven miles from the pole itself—before turning back. But it was the Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition, beginning in 1914, that defined his legend. When the Endurance was crushed by pack ice, Shackleton led his crew on an eight-hundred-mile journey across pack ice and open ocean to reach Elephant Island, where he left most of the team. Then he and five men made an eight-hundred-mile open ocean voyage in the tiny James Caird to reach South Georgia island, crossed its interior, and reached a whaling station to arrange rescue for everyone. That rescue of all twenty-eight men from what seemed certain death became the most extraordinary outcome of any expedition. Shackleton died in 1922 during a fourth Antarctic expedition, having become a legendary figure for leadership under impossible conditions.
